questions.question: Food, water, and housing are basic human needs.
questions.explanation: Basic needs are essential things required for survival, like nourishment, protection, and clothing.

questions.question: Why does our body need food and water?
options: To buy things at a shop
To have energy and function properly
To play with friends
To grow taller only
questions.explanation: Food and water provide the fuel and hydration necessary for our bodies to work and stay healthy.

questions.question: What does the word "needs" mean?
options: Things we want to have for fun
Things without which we can still function
Things that we need to live
Things that we buy once a year
questions.explanation: Needs are necessities that are vital for our existence and well-being.

questions.question: What does housing provide for us?
options: Safety and a place to rest
Entertainment and games
New clothes every week
Friends to play with
questions.explanation: A home provides shelter from the elements, security, and a space for recovery.

questions.question: Chrumko has very little money. Sort each item into the correct group.

dragTargets.label: Wait until there is enough money

questions.explanation: When money is limited, you should always prioritize needs (food, water) over wants (chocolate, toys).

questions.question: If Chrumko spends all his money on sweets and has nothing left for food, he made a good decision.
questions.explanation: Sweets are a luxury (want), while food is a necessity (need). Chrumko prioritized the wrong thing.

questions.question: Chrumko has a little money left. He can buy either bread and water, or a chocolate bar.
options: Buy the chocolate bar because it looks tastier.
Buy the bread and water first, since they are needs.
Buy nothing at all.
Buy the chocolate bar and worry about food later.
questions.explanation: Needs like food and water always come before wants like chocolate.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: Food and water are basic needs.
Housing gives us safety and a place to rest.
Spending all your money on sweets and having nothing for food is a good decision.
questions.explanation: Sweets are a want, not a need - spending everything on them instead of food is not a good decision.

questions.question: A want is something we can survive without.
questions.explanation: A want is something that makes life more pleasant but isn't required for survival.

questions.question: Match each item to whether it is a need or a want.
questions.explanation: Water and food are needs. A stuffed toy and fashion trainers are wants.

questions.question: Which statement best describes needs and wants?
options: Needs and wants are equally important
Wants are more important than needs
Needs are essential for survival; wants are not
Wants and needs are the same thing
questions.explanation: Needs are essential for survival; wants are not.

questions.question: Is it okay to have wants?
options: No, wants are always bad
No, we should only buy needs
Yes, and we should always fulfil them immediately
Yes, but we should know that needs are more important
questions.explanation: Wants are fine to have, as long as your basic needs are met first.

questions.question: If Chrumko wants a new toy but already has a similar one, that new toy is a need.
questions.explanation: Since he already has a toy that works, the new one is definitely a desire, not a necessity.

questions.question: Put the steps of smart decision-making in the correct order when Chrumko only has money for one thing.
orderItems: Chrumko finds a new toy, but his mom sent him to buy bread.
Is a new toy a necessity or a desire?
questions.explanation: Responsible money management means checking if your needs are covered before spending on anything else.

questions.question: Chrumko already has a toy car that works fine, but he sees a new one in the shop and wants it.
options: The new toy car is a want, since his old one still works.
The new toy car is a need, since he wants it so much.
He must buy it immediately.
Wanting something makes it automatically a need.
questions.explanation: Since his old toy still works, the new one is a want, not a need.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: A want is something we can survive without.
Needs are essential for survival; wants are not.
Wants are more important than needs and should always come first.
questions.explanation: Needs come before wants - wants are not more important.

lessons.lessonName: Why we want things we do not need

questions.question: When we want something the moment we see it, our brain is promising us a feeling of joy.
questions.explanation: Our brains often react to cool or shiny things by promising us a feeling of happiness if we get them.

questions.question: Match each influence to the type of pressure it creates.
matchLeft: A friend has a new toy
questions.explanation: We often want things because we see them in commercials or because our friends have them.

questions.question: Is there a difference between wanting and needing something?
options: There is no difference
Wanting something means you automatically need it too
Wanting and needing are two different feelings
Needing something is the same as wanting it
questions.explanation: Wanting something and needing something are two different feelings.

questions.question: If Chrumko's old pencil case still works, a new one is just a want.
questions.explanation: If the current item still performs its function, a new one is a want.

questions.question: Sort the reasons for why Chrumko did not buy the pencil case.
dragLabels: He realized he did not need it

dragTargets.label: Correct reason
correctItems: He realized he did not need it

questions.explanation: By thinking it over, Chrumko practiced good financial discipline by identifying it as an unnecessary want.

questions.question: Chrumko's pencil case still works fine, but he saw a friend with a new one and now wants one too.
options: This is a real need because his current one might break someday.
This is a want, triggered by seeing his friend's pencil case.
He must buy a new one right away to fit in.
Wanting it means the old one is now broken.
questions.explanation: Seeing a friend's item is a trigger for wanting things, but since his own pencil case still works, it's a want, not a need.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: Wanting something and needing something are two different feelings.
A TV advertisement can influence us to want something.
If an item still works, wanting a new one only happens because it is truly needed.
questions.explanation: If the old item still works, wanting a new one is driven by desire, not real need.

questions.question: The main goal of advertising is to persuade us that we need a product.
questions.explanation: Advertisements make things seem more appealing than they actually are.

questions.question: Match each advertising element to what it influences.
questions.explanation: Ads use sensory tricks to make products look and sound better than they might actually be.

questions.question: How do products in advertisements usually compare to real life?
options: Advertisers often show a perfect version that may differ from what you actually get
They always look exactly the same as in real life
They look worse than in real life
They always look exactly as described
questions.explanation: Advertisers often show the 'perfect' version of a product, which can be different from what you actually get.

questions.question: Put the steps in the correct order for what Chrumko should do before buying a product he saw in an ad.
orderItems: Stop and do not give in straight away
Compare the product to a real need
Decide based on facts, not the ad
questions.explanation: Smart shoppers look at the quality and the necessity of the item rather than the flashy packaging.

questions.question: Sort each statement under the correct label: advertisement or reality.
dragLabels: The chocolate is smaller than in the ad
The colors are edited by computer
The real taste may be different

dragTargets.label: Advertisement (what it promises)
correctItems: The colors are edited by computer

dragTargets.label: Reality (what you actually get)
correctItems: The chocolate is smaller than in the ad
The real taste may be different

questions.explanation: This is a common advertising tactic to make the product seem like a better deal than it is.

questions.question: Chrumko wants to buy something just because he saw it in an ad. What should he do?
options: Immediately find it and buy it
Ignore it because ads always lie
Think about whether he really needs it
Buy two
questions.explanation: You should always check if the desire comes from an actual need or just the influence of a clever ad.

questions.question: Chrumko sees an ad for a toy that looks huge and amazing on screen.
options: He should assume the real toy will look exactly the same.
He should remember ads often show a 'perfect' version that may differ from reality.
He should buy two, since ads never lie.
He should ignore whether he actually needs it.
questions.explanation: Things in advertisements don't always look the same in real life.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: The main goal of advertising is to persuade us that we need a product.
Bright colors and upbeat music in ads can influence our feelings about a product.
Products in advertisements always look exactly the same as they do in real life.
questions.explanation: Advertising often exaggerates reality.

questions.question: Strong emotions such as anger or sadness never lead to impulse purchases.
questions.explanation: Strong emotions impair our ability to make rational decisions, which is why we often act impulsively.

questions.question: Why do we sometimes buy things when we are sad?
options: Because we need them to survive
Because we must
Because they are cheap
Because they can bring short-term joy
questions.explanation: Buying something new releases chemicals in the brain that make us feel better for a little while.

questions.question: What is usually true about emotional purchases?
options: They are always based on real needs
They always save money
They are always a good idea
They are rarely based on real needs
questions.explanation: Decisions based purely on feelings often lead to regret once the emotion fades.

questions.question: Match each situation to the correct response.
matchLeft: Chrumko is angry and wants a sweet
Chrumko is sad and very thirsty
Chrumko is excited and wants an expensive toy
matchRight: Buy water - it is a need
Buy food - it is a need
questions.explanation: Tell the difference between real needs and impulses driven by emotion.

questions.question: Chrumko is sad and very thirsty and wants to buy water. What should he do?
options: Buy it immediately
Wait until he is no longer sad
Not buy anything to save money
Spend all his money on food
questions.explanation: Even if he is sad, thirst is a biological need. He should buy the water because it is a necessity.

questions.question: Sort the reasons for Chrumko's decision not to buy anything.
dragLabels: He did not need anything else

dragTargets.label: Correct reason
correctItems: He did not need anything else

questions.explanation: Chrumko realized that since he wasn't hungry, buying food wasn't a current need.

questions.question: Chrumko is angry after losing a game and suddenly wants to buy a big bag of sweets.
options: He should buy it immediately since he is upset.
He should wait, since strong emotions like anger can lead to impulsive purchases.
Anger always means he truly needs sweets.
He should buy even more to feel better longer.
questions.explanation: Strong emotions like anger can cloud judgment and lead to impulsive purchases - it's best to wait until the emotion passes.

questions.question: One of these statements is wrong. Find it.
options: If Chrumko is sad and thirsty, he should never buy water because thirst is not a real need.
Strong emotions like anger or sadness can lead to impulsive purchases.
Emotional purchases are rarely based on real needs.
questions.explanation: Thirst is a biological need - even if he's sad, buying water is buying something he truly needs.
